entries.label: The Warm Furrow
entries.text: Dawn smelled of frost and wet fur. Boof put her nose to the ground and read the field the way she read it every morning. Everything was where it belonged. The latch lifted at the kitchen. The bucket knocked the well. A blackbird tried the same few notes until one pleased it. Beneath the berry rows, the ants kept their little hearths, and their patient magic warmed the roots through winter; above them, the boonberries slept under ice, each holding a drop of light. On the coldest nights, when the frost split a furrow, you could see the hearths at work: a pin of light no bigger than a seed, carried down along a root by something with more legs than Boof cared to count, and behind it another, and another, a whole small procession going home along streets no map had room for. Boof did not dig. Some business is not a dog's, and the ants had never once asked her for anything. Boof followed the rows past the fence that leaned into last year's weeds, past the place where the miller always stopped to scrape his boots. She sniffed a root here and there, and the field gave back its usual answers. Boof knew this field. She worked for the land, wherever the fences stood. Nobody paid her, and nobody had needed to; the land kept her the way it kept the ants, without either side signing anything. She did not especially like blueberries. She appreciated them, which is a different thing, and which the field seemed to know. She sniffed. Stepped. Stopped. One furrow was warm. Too warm. Beneath it, the ants had stopped working. Or not stopped — gathered, the way they gather at a hearth when a new coal is laid. Boof dug. First frost, then soft earth, then a little cloud of steam. At the bottom lay an egg the size of a curled cat, dark as an old lamp. She touched it with one paw. It hummed. No nest. No tracks. No mother-scent. She went around the hole once more, slowly. Whatever had brought it here had left no way to follow. Inside the shell, an unspent wish waited. Boof heard only the hum.

entries.label: Boof
entries.text: Ant-warmth smelled earthy and even, like bread left under a cloth. This was sharper. A candle just blown out. Boof knew the paths to the kitchens, the mill, and the grove nobody liked to name after dark. She had never found an egg on any of them. Certainly not one that warmed a whole furrow. She rested her chin on the rim of the hole. The egg hummed against the earth. Under her chin, she felt it answer. She would have preferred a trail. Trails usually ended with something you could eat.

entries.label: When a Berry Remembers
entries.text: Every boonberry had been a blueberry once. A wish had passed over it on the way to being granted, leaving a little of its light behind. Most slept through everything: snow, crows, harvest. The town used them for supper and lanterns. Nobody ate one warm. By the time a boonberry reached a table it had given its light to a lamp or a pie, and what was left was sweet and ordinary. Boof had never wondered what the light was for. She had been busy. The berry nearest the egg shed its frost. A gold seam opened in its skin. Its light leaned toward the shell, then past it, down the slope. The next berry turned. Then the next. Row by row, a low glow led toward the grove. Boof followed with her nose. The berries remembered this hum. Long ago, it had passed them going the other way. She looked back at the hole. Something had come home. Why had nobody come to fetch it?

entries.label: The Maps That Look Away
entries.text: Before the frost was off the fences, Boof had carried the egg to the map-house in an old feed-sack. It was warm as a loaf and considerably heavier. She set it on the reading table. The archivist fetched a book. Along a fold in the map, two roads touched. Boof knew those roads. A day's walk lay between them. Outside, a cart bell rang beneath the window. The archivist smoothed the fold. The bell dwindled to a far, thin chime. Boof lifted her head. The archivist put a stone on the crease. Neither looked away first. Then he tried to enter the egg in the book. Egg, one. Dawnward field. Unclaimed. The ink gathered into beads and rolled off the page. He tried a second pen. Boof waited. Maps keep what has happened. An unspent wish has not happened yet, and the page had nowhere to put it. The archivist wiped the table. Boof watched the stone. That, at least, he had known how to hold down.

entries.label: Following the Hum
entries.text: Outside, the berries still leaned toward the grove. Boof had spent the morning asking a book. The field had been pointing all along. She settled the feed-sack against her chest, where a pup might ride. A fine gold crack had opened at the egg's crown. It looked like a door left slightly ajar. The hum kept its steady measure. Her paws found another. Down the slope. Past the last row. At the edge of the field she paused. Behind her stood a house full of maps. Ahead lay the way the berries remembered. She went ahead.

entries.label: Boof
entries.text: Evening laid long light across the field. Boof was hungry. The egg was warm. For a while, that was all. Behind her, the berries glowed under their leaves. Ahead, the first trees crowded close. Then a sound came out of the grove. HONK. Long, bent, and rather pleased with itself. Like a goose that had learned jazz. Boof stopped with one paw raised. The egg's hum slipped into time with it. She waited for a second note. Leaves stirred. Nothing more. She put her paw down and entered the trees.

entries.label: A Beat Late
entries.text: By the second morning, warmth had worked through sack and strap and settled against Boof's ribs. Behind her, the town maps still showed an ordinary field. Ahead, the berries' remembered route ran into birch and fern, where the air smelled damp—and somehow twice breathed. She stopped beneath the first tree. Nothing moved. Something arrived again. She laid the egg on a mossy stone. Pollen hung in rings between the trunks, catching the light; her breath went out and came back thin, a little late. Then the hum returned. Again. Each time it carried something different: rain on leaves, the smell of supper, a door opening onto a morning she almost knew. The grove was trying out futures. None had happened yet. Boof listened until she could pick the returns apart. One came from the hollow cedar, low and round; another thinned among the birches; a third seemed to start behind her teeth. She closed her mouth. It came again. The egg lay still on its stone, and the moss beneath it had begun to dry. She looked from that small pale patch to the trembling gold in the air. So much happening overhead, and down here one egg warming one stone. She kept a paw beside it, where she could feel which of them was real.

entries.label: Boof
entries.text: The leaning berries had led her here—the grove beyond the last honest furrow, a place the town labeled as reserve growth and the workers called the listening thicket. Every step pressed an unfinished fragment out of the leaf-mold. Half a lullaby somebody stopped singing. The first word of a prayer nobody dared finish. A clerk saying no such entry, with the hollow confidence of someone who had never carried a want too small to say out loud. no such entry with the hollow confidence of someone who had never carried a wanting too small to say out loud. Boof knew how towns worked. When a record-house is too clean, the wanting does not vanish; it drains downhill into the wild growth, where nobody asks what you came for. This thicket was where Boon.land kept every wish it preferred not to admit to having, every note it wanted to sound and didn't.

entries.label: Boonberry
entries.text: The berries here did not shine for the harvest. They were the wild cousins of the field rows: blueberries a wish had passed over long ago, each holding its drop of the granting. In the thicket they pulsed like grains under stress — bright when an echo rehearsed a future they remembered the taste of, dim when the thicket put them back to sleep. Boof recognized several of her own past silences reflected in the dark skins of the fruit—small wantings she had swallowed instead of sounding. That was the grove's first cruelty: it kept what the town preferred not to admit to. Unspent wants. Unsounded notes. And no ants kept this ground. No torch-lines ran along the roots; no small city held the winter off. The wild rows grew cold and stubborn, living off whatever heat the echoes left behind, which was why their light flickered instead of holding.

entries.label: Echo
entries.text: "Follow me," said an echo that used Boof's own pitch from years earlier—the careful, hopeful voice she had used back when she still asked for things instead of working for them. The path forked around an ancient hollow cedar and rejoined on the other side. Time here did not reverse; it rehearsed. In the suspended dust of the pollen rings there was always a second egg, a breath behind the first, shivering in gold spores—the wish trying out a future where it had already been granted, then setting the future back down, unconvinced, and trying the next one.

entries.label: What the Echo Keeps
entries.text: Boof paced the fork, nose to moss, while the grove offered rain, harvest, a road back to a better morning. Each future fitted nearly. That was the trouble. The wish stayed warm through all of them, and the hum kept coming back for another try. She could spend her whole life here listening to almost. She took up the sling. In the pollen, the other egg lingered a breath behind, then stayed where it was. Boof walked on. Downhill, damp bark gave way to salt air; under the sand, something older had begun to answer. She listened without turning back.

entries.label: The Fool
entries.text: Three wishes, says the old song. Wrong count, says the Fool. Three COMPLETED wishes — a wish isn't granted till it's finished. He leaned out of a cedar where no door had been cut, pollen on mismatched sleeves, one hand cupped to his mouth like a brass bell. He'd been the honk in the treeline, of course. He sampled the trope the way you’d lift a plate off a stranger’s table. “You know this one: a lamp, a rub, three wishes, and a fool who wastes the third un-wishing the first.” Then he sounded it — HONK, one long bent note — and handed it back changed: the song never counts the finishing. Anybody can start a wish. Starting is cheap. The grove is full of starts. What costs, what really costs, is the last word, said out loud, with your whole weight on it. Every trope you sample, he said, tipping an invisible hat to the egg, must be returned changed, with interest. Boof did not answer with a riddle, and she opened no book. She wrote the grove's first usable note on the air with her nose: an echo is a wish rehearsing; a rehearsal is not a granting; a granting needs a finisher. Then she trotted past him into the sand, because somewhere out there was whoever had left a wish one word short, and the trail smelled like the only honest question left.

entries.label: Boof
entries.text: The grove fell away behind her into a vast, wind-scoured plain of dry salt and baked earth. Boof stood at the edge of the Fool's Paradox . The crust forked and would not be two places at once. Under the rippled dunes, two older routes glowed like habits the land had never broken, both wanting the same next step—two directions of travel that had spent so many years almost meeting that they had worn a want of their own into the ground. The egg against her ribs hummed louder whenever she faced the seam, the way a wish leans toward other unfinished things. A leaning wooden signpost stood half-swallowed by drift-sand. Its painted lettering had flaked off seasons ago, but its long evening shadow stretched across the flats like an unyielding black needle. At the tip of the shadow, right where the two routes wanted to become one turn, a curve of green glass broke the crust. Boof dug. The flats gave up a bottle, stoppered, sand-scoured, and warm in the way of a chair somebody has only just left.

entries.label: Paradox
entries.text: The stopper turned. Steam rose, folded, found sleeves. Out came the Off-Season Genie, neat as a handkerchief and dressed like a clerk on his first day without a desk. He looked from egg to dog to glowing sand. “Two routes. One turn. Used to settle these before breakfast.” A wish, he explained, redirected what was already moving. These routes had been nearly meeting for a century. One coincidence and a Thursday would have done it. He brushed his cuffs. “Of course, I'm closed.” The egg was the last unfinished wish from the practice he'd shut down; he recognized it at once and looked away a moment too late.

entries.label: The Fool
entries.text: You know the trope: rub the lamp, mind the fine print. HONK. The fine print was never the trap. The wholesale price was. The Fool trotted backward down the dune, spinning an empty brass lamp on one finger. He had sampled the old song of genies, and he handed it back changed. It was never three wishes and a catch, he honked. It was a price list all along, and the grand wishes were the loss leaders. Footprints filled with sand the moment his heels lifted.

entries.label: The Seam in the Sand
entries.text: The Genie laid his instruments on the sand: a scale, a long glass, a brass needle quick to find a want. He had made emperors with these. Moved rivers. Unmade two emperors at cost. Boof sat still. The scale stayed level; the glass showed fruit and fields; the needle circled, slowed, and tried again. “Below my resolution,” he said. “Emperors want loudly. Ants want small, but there are so many of them, all wanting the same warm inch, that it comes to a loud sound in the end. I did good business with ants. You appear to want—” He tapped the glass. “Something these don't show.” He cleaned the lens on his sleeve, although there was no dust on it. Boof waited with the patience she used beside a cupboard someone had forgotten opening. The needle caught a glint of evening, pointed briefly toward the bottle, then swung away. The Genie moved the bottle behind him. Neither mentioned it. Across the flats the wind brushed their footprints shallow, and the two old routes continued their long, unfinished turn. For all his instruments, he had no measure for the length of this particular silence. Boof huffed and looked at the seam, where two old routes still leaned toward each other like tired dancers. Could he not simply grant the turn, seal the wish, mend the map? "I'm not saying no," said the Genie. "I'm saying reality is already moving very quickly in another direction, and every correction has to come out of somewhere. Perfect version costs a miracle. Mediocre version costs one coincidence and a Thursday. Your version—" and here his voice did something it had not done in years, which was lift "—I can't price your version. I can't even read it." A want too small for the instruments of empire. He had liquidated his whole practice without ever once seeing one.

entries.label: Boof
entries.text: Boof huffed and walked between the routes, paws in the seam, her weight enough to give their leaning somewhere to go. Behind her the two lines settled into one turn. A long-held chord came home. No miracle was billed. The Genie watched the dust settle over work he would have charged a Thursday for. "I'm coming with you," he said, tucking the bottle under one arm. "Not to grant anything. Understand that. I am closed." But a want too small to read had just done, for free, what he would have billed a Thursday for, and a small want was the one wonder his price list had never carried. Ahead, where the desert gave way to scrub and rising stone, Council Hill lifted its stormy silhouette against the evening sky. The egg hummed against Boof's ribs, one word short of finished, and the three of them—dog, wish, and the only professional who had ever refused to guess it—walked toward the hill together.

entries.label: Boof
entries.text: Council Hill kept a great slab of split pine that refused to pick a side, and it was there, under crosswind weather, that Boof brought the egg to be argued over. She slipped beneath the trestle, chin on the timber, and found herself nose to frame with the Fool’s Mirror —an upright pane of polished weather that returned not your face but the exact shape of your wanting. Above her, the law of the hill was recited as it had been recited for generations: every permission in Boon.land is a key, iron or brass, and a key may be filed smaller in the open, before witnesses, with the shavings swept into the common bin. A key may never be grown in secret. The Genie stood at the table's edge, hands folded, and added the one fact that mattered: a wish is the largest key ever cut. It opens the momentum of the world itself. That was when the bane-side chair creaked. The bitter pie arrived by hired cart, lattice crust tight over berries he'd kept too long. He offered nobody a slice. The wish, he proposed, should be valued, filed, and sold to someone prepared to bear its considerable responsibilities. He paused to let the council imagine such a person. Then supplied his own name.

entries.label: Mirror
entries.text: The Fool’s Mirror shimmered with the fury of the split sky. It whispered in a tone like wind through eaves: "What you see is not what is, but what your wanting is becoming." The delegates looked, one by one. The boon-side saw their small wants, snug as filed keys. Mr. BaneWAP looked longest, and the glass returned him honestly: every berry he had ever hoarded, pressed airless under crust, gone from sweet to bitter for want of being served. He was not a villain from elsewhere. He was the mirror of what wanting becomes when it stops handing out slices. The egg, reflected beside him, showed no bidder's number and no bounding box — a wish keeps its own law, and no appraisal on the hill could get purchase on its shell.

entries.label: The Fool
entries.text: Every court gets a vizier. I sampled that trope, folks — and honked it back as pastry. One-footed on the unsigned auction ledger, the Fool produced a small hot hand-pie from nowhere polite and set it before Mr. BaneWAP with a bow. The whisperer-at-the-throne, the schemer in the sleeve — an old trope, sampled a thousand times. He returned it changed, with interest: in Boon.land the vizier is baked goods, and you can smell exactly what he's been hoarding.

entries.label: No Key Covers the Egg
entries.text: Boof watched the argument cross the pine grain like weather. Boon and bane sat under one shared squall and bargained without declaring war; that was the table's whole genius. But when the clerks brought out the rack of civic keys — iron ones honestly narrowed, brass ones watched for secret growing — not one of them matched the egg. The Genie explained it the way he priced everything, flatly and without pity: a wish is not property, because it is not a thing; it is a redirection of momentum the world already has. You cannot auction a bend in the river. You can only stand where it bends. From beneath the table, Boof could see the parts of the meeting the mirror missed: wet hems, boots braced against the slope, a clerk warming cramped fingers under one arm. Whenever a delegate struck the pine, dust shook loose beside her nose. They wanted the rain kept off their roofs and the paths kept open to their doors; some wanted more, but those wants were there beneath the grander words. She shifted the egg away from a drip. Above her, someone asked who would be responsible for keeping it safe. None of the keys fitted. The oldest clerk tried the last one, set it down, and wrote: the wish stays with its finder. Rain ticked on the tabletop. Across it, the pie smiled. “And who,” he asked, “inherits from the finder?” Boof's fur lifted along her back. The clerk kept his pen above the page.

entries.label: Boof
entries.text: Boof left the hill with the wish she had never asked to hold. Finder, the clerk had written, as if finding were a small thing a dog did with her nose and not a door the world had opened under her paws. The Genie walked beside her, unhurried. "He will not steal it," he said of the pie on the other road. "Stealing costs a miracle. Paperwork costs pocket change, and he knows which one he can afford." Below the hill, two claims reached the hall of arches before supper. One named Boof. One called the wish an asset. The clerks pinned them side by side, shut the door, and went home. Under the desk, where no one thought to listen, the floor began to sing.

entries.label: Boof
entries.text: The hall under the tall stone arches was calm the way a drawn bowstring is calm. Sunlight lay across cedar shelves and a long desk worn pale by elbows, and across the slate floor ran a hairline crack that hummed. Boof padded in on quiet paws, following the vibration before she could hear it — the Fool’s Song running the crack like a held breath. Two slips hung over the desk, pinned with silver bodkins, and both of them were pulling. One was the boon-claim: the wish belongs to whoever found it, and through her to everyone. The other had arrived at first light in Mr. BaneWAP's crust-brown envelope, sealed twice and smelling faintly of sour pastry: the wish is a thing, and things belong to whoever can hold them longest. Each slip leaned toward the egg in Boof's sling. The egg leaned toward neither. Below the desk its warmth found the hairline, and the floor began, very quietly, to part. The silence in the room was not peaceful. It was the silence of two wants holding the same breath, kept only because nobody had dared to let it go.

entries.label: Song
entries.text: The song climbed the rafters by a narrow stair of notes. One rose for a wish shared out; one held for a wish locked away. Together they made a sound Boof could feel in her teeth. She shifted her paw. The crack ran on beneath it. Whatever the slips said, the floor could not keep both promises.

entries.label: The Fool
entries.text: Two receipts on one warmth — the oldest quarrel on the shelf. Somebody wished big here once, and the floor is still paying the note. The tuning fork hummed against the split desk. The wood, not the Fool, was singing — a very old melody, in a key nobody had budgeted for.

entries.label: Wish-Physics Over the Crack
entries.text: The Genie stood astride the crack. “A cart rolling. Rain falling. A Thursday on its way. A wish can turn those.” He nudged a loose edge of slate. “Ask for a little turn, pay a little. Ask the world to swing around you, and somebody else catches the weight.” Long ago, someone had wished grandly here. Gold, perhaps. A throne. Nobody remembered the wish. The crack remembered its weight. “Still paying,” he said. Under his slipper, the note went on. The egg did not pick a side. A wish keeps its own law; it is not there to settle other people's wanting. Its heat kept the hairline open and honest, so no one could smooth the seam over with wax and a confident voice and call the quarrel finished. Boof left both slips where they hung, pulling at nothing, and turned toward the western gate — toward the city that had learned to turn its old breakages into light. A little dried ink clung to the edge of the desk. Boof watched it quiver when the note rose, then rest when it fell. The room had been swept with care. Pens lay straight; the stools were tucked away; whoever worked here had tried to leave things ready for morning. Yet the crack ran beneath all that order, passing under the stool where someone would sit and between the shelves where someone would reach. She could follow it farther than she could see. Somewhere beyond the wall, a cup began to rattle.

entries.label: Boof
entries.text: Boof understood the physics better than the hall did, because she had lived it at bowl-height her whole life. A dog who works for the land knows you cannot wish a bowl full; you can only be standing under the bush when the fruit was already going to fall. Redirect, don't create. Her wants had always been small enough to afford. She had simply never known that was a kind of wealth. Out in the avenue, the thin song faded into footfall, wheel-rattle, evening trade. Boof kept the egg close. Ahead, Bonk City's windows caught the last light: old impacts melted into glass, a skyline of things that had been struck and still let someone see through.

entries.label: Boof
entries.text: Boof trotted into Bonk City the way you step into the acoustic chamber of a struck bell. The streets did not follow straight surveyor lines; they formed a Fool’s Labyrinth of curving bronze posts, rain-slick arches, and leaning panes. The glass of Bonk City was not quarried or blown from river sand alone: it was made of old impacts, every collision the city had ever survived melted down and clarified, so that the panes remembered being struck and had forgiven it into transparency. The lanterns were honest in the one way that mattered — they showed light without claiming to be it. Every one of them turned its faceted face toward the warm egg in her sling, casting its heat across the cobbles while owning not a single ember of the flame. And ahead, down the widest winding street, the smell of boonberries baking rose over the rooftops like a second dusk — because the patron of Bonk City was holding court, and the patron of Bonk City is a pie.

entries.label: Labyrinth
entries.text: “Every pane will offer you your own warmth,” said a voice behind the glass. Boof turned. Three reflections turned with her. “Very flattering. Very little supper.” She lifted her nose. Through the rain and brass came the smell of crust. “There you are,” said the voice. “Glass can show a flame. It can't bake a pie.”

entries.label: The Fool
entries.text: A lantern is a bruise that learned to give directions. From the lamplighter’s top rung he tapped the brass bell into a crease, and the post remembered heat. Old impact, sampled; returned as light, with interest. That, he remarked to no one and everyone, is the whole city in one honk.

entries.label: The Pie at the Table
entries.text: Every street eventually arrived at a round plaza. At its center, on an oak table, a warm boonberry pie held court. Rain had followed them into the plaza in the folds of coats and the soles of shoes. It steamed from the porters' shoulders while they ate. Boof settled where she could watch the table legs and the lanes between them, the dropped crumb, the swinging heel, a spoon rescued before it reached the stones. Above her, conversation passed with the plates. Somebody had lost a button; somebody knew a shortcut home. Between courses a porter unrolled something on the table's edge for the child to see: a page pressed flat under a sheet of Bonk glass, thin as a leaf and warm from his coat. Under the glass a drawn hill, a drawn dog, a smear where rain had once got in before the glassing and been kept there, forgiven. He turned it over. A second page lay glassed beneath the first, older, with the same hill drawn smaller. They called them folios, he told the child, and you glassed one whenever the story changed, over the last one, so nothing you had known was lost, only layered. Boof put her nose to the edge. It smelled of pressure and heat and, faintly, of the day it was made. The egg warmed her chest, the ovens warmed her face, and for a little while she could sit among people whose largest unanswered question was whether to have another slice. The knife went in. A slice came out. The pie stayed whole. Boof watched it happen eleven times. A lamplighter ate. A porter took seconds. A child who ought to have been asleep licked the plate. Boof checked beneath the table. No second pie. A server set down another plate and rubbed her wrist. “Enough for everyone,” she told Boof. “Always.” She looked at the washing-up. Boof got off the stool. The server sat. Steam rose from the crust. The pie considered the egg. “If you spent the wish tonight, what would you ask?” Boof opened her mouth. A furrow. A door. The smell of next spring. She could feel the want, but couldn't get its pieces into words. She shut her mouth again. “Good,” said the pie. “Still proofing.” At the far gate, something lattice-crusted shifted in the dark. “Take it out too soon,” he added, more quietly, “and see what you get.”

entries.label: Boof
entries.text: Boof paused at the last curb of the labyrinth and shook the rain from her ears. She carried a slice of BoonWAP wrapped in waxed paper, and the pie behind her was exactly as large as before, and her wish was still wordless and rising somewhere behind her ribs, and all of that was, apparently, correct. She had not eaten the slice. It was warm through the paper, and she was saving it. She could not have said for what. The glass had shown her light without claiming it. The pie had fed a plaza without shrinking. There were ways of being warm in this world that did not require owning the heat. She stepped past the last glowing pane into the quiet square. Under the open stars waited an ancient stone slab with a deep circular groove carved into its granite top: the place where oaths are given in public and paid in the honest currency of fruit. The wheel-tracks in the dew ahead of her smelled of hoarded berries. BaneWAP had left the gates before her, and he had come this way.

entries.label: Boof
entries.text: The great market stone stood at the center of the square, its granite top worn smooth and dished by centuries of pressing palms. Boof had come to do the one thing the council could not do for her and BaneWAP could not undo: bind herself, in public, to the wish. For an oath here was understood exactly as the Genie had taught her to understand keys — it was a key given away in daylight , handed to the whole watching town at once, so that no one hand could ever secretly grow it. The public half was the words. The private half was paid in fruit, pressed into the rock where centuries of sworn juice had gone before. And the witness was the egg itself, set warm upon the lip of the stone: an unspent wish, watching a promise being made about its own spending. Boof pressed a blueberry into the stone. Skin split; juice slipped into the groove worn by other paws and palms. She would spend the wish when the want was true. Not for spite, not for show. Not because a crowd was waiting. The square fell quiet enough to hear a stall-cloth flap. Beneath her other paw, the egg grew warmer.

entries.label: Shadow
entries.text: But every oath sworn in noon light casts one. The shadow lay across the grooves, dog-shaped, egg-shaped, cold, and it was not BaneWAP's — it was the oath's own dark half, the clause nobody reads aloud. The Genie read it anyway, because pricing things was the one habit he had not liquidated. "Understand what you have promised to spend," he said quietly. "A wish redirects momentum. Redirected momentum lands somewhere. Every spent wish — mine, yours, anyone's — owes one coincidence to a stranger. A cart delayed, a letter misdelivered, a rain moved to a different field. Someone always pays the correction, and they are never at the ceremony."

entries.label: The Fool
entries.text: The sworn oath — oldest trope on the shelf. Kings swear on swords. She swore on fruit. Returned with interest. From the awning he laid it out like a set: the hero's vow, sampled from every saga that ever rattled a mead-hall — swords kissed, blood mingled, thrones promised. He honked it back changed: no blade, no blood, one blueberry, one working dog, and a clause the sagas always skipped — the stranger's bill. That was the interest. An oath that admits its shadow is worth ten that don't.

entries.label: The Shadow Price
entries.text: After the crowd thinned, Boof stayed, chin against the granite. Purple juice dried beside older stains. Somewhere, a stranger would be late because she had wished: a cart missed, a letter lost, rain on the wrong field. She could neither find them nor warn them. The oath gave her no way around that. She sat until the stone cooled beneath her chin. Around her, the square returned to its smaller business. A merchant shook rain from an awning, a child chased a rolling spool, and two neighbors resumed an argument they had set aside for the ceremony. None of them knew which stranger would catch the turn of her wish. Perhaps that stranger was having an ordinary afternoon too, expecting a letter, counting the hours to supper. Boof watched the spool lodge between two stones. The child knelt to free it. She stayed a little longer, until the crowd had become people again. She pressed one last blueberry into the central groove until the purple juice welled up and filled the old gold-veined cracks. Payment that smelled true. The lattice-edged shadow at the alley mouth withdrew without a sound — an oath witnessed in public is a poor thing to bid on. Boof lifted the egg back into her sling and turned her nose south, toward the ancient well that keeps every face without stealing a single soul.

entries.label: The Fool
entries.text: Swear small, pay in fruit, and tip the stranger you will never meet. His voice thinned with the market bell. Stalls folded, shadows lengthened, and far away a cart kept someone waiting. No one in the square heard its driver call.

entries.label: Boof
entries.text: The Watering Eye was a well before it was a witness, and a witness long before anyone built a tavern leaning over it like a drinker over a confession. Boof came in under the sagging floorboards and set her front paws on the mossy coping. The water below was black and perfectly still, and it did not show her own face first. It showed her an older one — a woman mid-wish, mouth open on a want she had never said aloud — and under that face, folded like pressed linen going down into the dark, every other face the well had ever held. From the barrel-head behind her came the Genie's quoting voice , brisk as a market morning: "I can make you famous by Tuesday, or respected by November. Fame is cheap — reality already leans that way for loud people. Respect requires corrections. Choose." A face said into deep water is not stolen; it is folded, and it stays the property of whoever wore it. The well kept the faces the way good ground keeps rain: patiently, and without letting anyone else spend them.

entries.label: Fold
entries.text: All night the Genie dealt in wants. Name one, hear the price, pay or fold. An empire? Quite manageable; the world was forever tipping toward a throne. Supper everyone agreed on? He counted the company twice and quoted three coincidences and a fortnight of Thursdays. At the bar, the regular raised his glass. “Six violations of the natural order,” the Genie told him. “Lager,” said the regular. The Genie wrote it down. After a moment, he underlined it. A line of ants had left a crumb on the barrel-head at dusk. He quoted them nothing, struck a match for their torch-bearer, and wrote nothing down. Old customers. Two beavers took the whole evening over a dam. They wanted the wording exact: the bend, the height, the arrangement of the sticks. By the time they had it right they had drawn it on the table in spilled lager, argued the drawing into a better one, and gone out to build it before the Genie could quote a price. He watched them go with something like professional respect. Beavers, he told Boof, always wished slowly enough to finish the job themselves.

entries.label: The Fool
entries.text: Eighth honk: the tavern game, sampled and returned — small wants priced dear, because they are the ones the world was not already planning to grant. He sat the trapdoor's edge with his boots over the dark, tapping the game's rhythm on the iron ring, taking the tavern's off-key song and handing it back on-key, with interest.

entries.label: The Unpriceable Want
entries.text: Near closing, he tried Boof again. “Anything. Name it.” She thought of the furrow, the warmth, a trail with something real at its end. His needle swung beyond the numbers and came back blank. He reset it. She tried again. Same small click, same empty dial. Boof lowered the egg onto the wet stone around the well. Heat spread under her paws, through the coping, down. The folded faces stirred. One by one they turned toward the warmth the way the berries once had. Then the water said, in the plain way water says things, what every face down there had in common: each one owed a coincidence to a stranger. The egg — an unspent wish — was the debt still standing warm above the fold. The well could not price it either. It only named it, and kept the account open. Boof leaned over the rim without touching the water. Some faces were clear enough to count the lines around a mouth; others drifted beneath reflections of the tavern windows. A laugh came through the floorboards overhead, and for a moment she could not tell whether one of the faces had laughed too. She moved the egg closer. Ripples reached the far wall and came back through the reflected light. The Genie stood beside her with his instruments shut. She was glad he had stopped asking her to name it.

entries.label: Boof
entries.text: "What did I win?" Boof wondered, taking the egg back into her sling. The Genie had priced fame, thrones, and six lagers, and had folded on her — the only player at the table whose want his game could not hold. Behind her the regular raised one finger at the dark, on principle. She climbed toward the roofs with the well's answer warming her ribs. The egg was a debt. The faces below had turned toward it together, though no voice had called them. Above the ridge, eight old notes hung in the dark. She listened for the missing one and felt it humming against her chest.

entries.label: Boof
entries.text: The Fool had an art, and on the ridge above the town he finally showed Boof its bones. He laid his set out on the slates shard by shard — a lineage in nine pieces — for the unit of the art is the honk: a trope sampled from the old tales, sounded in a new mouth, and returned changed, with interest. Each shard hummed the shape of the story it was cut from, and as he set them down in a crescent, Boof could hear where every chamber of their road had come from and where it had been sent back richer. The law of it is short enough for a dog to carry: every trope you sample must be returned changed, with interest. A honk that only repeats is a debt; a honk that returns is a harvest.

entries.label: Shard
entries.text: The Fool laid out the shards. Three wishes; a trickster in a tree; a genie lately out of business. A vizier, baked bitter. Two claims splitting a floor. Glass streets, a blueberry oath, a tavern game that couldn't price its quietest player. He touched each piece as he named it, letting the little rings overlap. “Eight.” He slid them together. One space remained. Boof looked at the space, then down at her sling.

entries.label: The Fool
entries.text: The ninth honk was never sounded. An unspent wish is an unsounded note — and the set was built around its silence. On the chimney rim he breathed through an empty mouthpiece. Steam came out. Not sound. Not yet.

entries.label: The Shape with One Hole
entries.text: The egg fitted without a push. Eight shards answered together, their separate sounds drawing into one hum. Boof felt it through her nose. Here were the places she had walked, close enough to touch, with a space for what she still carried. The Fool let her look. For once, he had nothing to add. The slates still held the day's warmth. Below them, somebody was closing shutters, one clap after another down the street, while a late cart worked its way toward the gate. Boof could have followed any of those sounds to an ordinary evening. Instead she stayed with the pieces. This one caught the light like the grove; that edge brought back the hard feel of the market stone beneath her paw. They made a shape together, but she remembered the distance between them, the meals and mud and waiting. No one could have handed her that at the beginning. "A honk is spent breath," the Fool said, lifting the egg free and settling it back in her sling. "A wish is breath still held. Same lineage, opposite ends." The ninth honk would sound when the wish was spent — no sooner, and by the Blueberry Oath, not before the want was true. She left the eight shards singing softly on the rooftop and turned down toward the northern pass, where the great timber spine of Bone.land waited to be asked what a small thing can hold.

entries.label: Boof
entries.text: Down the ridge, Boof carried the unsounded note against her ribs. The others could stay on the roof and sing to the chimneys. This one needed walking. She had promised to wait until the want was true; now she knew the silence had been waiting with her. She did not need the eight shards to know her place in the lineage. She had the ninth, folded in its shell against her ribs, and it was leading straight into the massive timber spine of Bone.land, where nothing is trusted until it has proved it can bear weight.

entries.label: Boof
entries.text: Bone.land did not pretend to be theater. Its square-hewn oak beams rose into the morning like the ribcage of a sleeping leviathan, every mortise and peg left exposed to the weather, because this hall was the small constitution — the spine the land trusted to hold when the veil shakes. Boof trotted across the sawdust floor, and the whole valley heard the frame answer her arrival with one deep BONK — not slapstick, but the sound of a structure declaring itself load-bearing. And on a scrubbed trestle table between the anchor stones sat something new: a pale, plain pie, steaming faintly, ringed by plumb lines and tuning pegs. "Mx. BoneWAP," it said, by way of everything. "Load-bearing. I listen to what things will carry. Set the wish on the frame, please." Where BaneWAP was hoarded berries gone bitter in a banker's crust, and BoonWAP served himself and was never smaller, BoneWAP was clean-boiled honesty: no sugar it had not declared, no filling it could not show. In Bone.land, even a pie keeps its joints exposed.

entries.label: Bonk
entries.text: The egg went onto the frame. A weight slid, a beam settled, and a low note ran through the frame into Boof's paws. The answer came up through the wood in gold: the smallest wishes have the longest arcs. Given the current, a small turn could travel generations. Force the whole river round a throne and the corrections would come downstream, roof by roof. Boof shook the ringing from her ears. It stayed in the wood.

entries.label: The Fool
entries.text: Plaster sneezes. Oak does not. Grand wishes are plaster; small ones are the spine. He hung from the collar-beam like a bright bat and knocked. The oak answered as law, and the pie below him signed it.

entries.label: What the Frame Would Bear
entries.text: BoneWAP did not whisper the answer to a council or fold it into a drawer. It let the hall ring — and a hall that size, struck true, is heard in every kitchen of the valley. By noon the note had gone out on the pass road, to the tavern, to the Watering Eye, where people said it back to one another. The Egg’s wish, spent small and true, would cost one lent coincidence and a spare Thursday, and its arc would outlast every roof in the valley. The grand wish a certain bitter pie intended would call in a generation of coincidences — a whole town’s luck, drawn without asking. People stopped to hear it with baskets on their arms and tools still in their hands. Some hummed the note to check it; some asked a neighbor to say it again. It traveled out of the hall in voices that sounded nothing alike. Boof heard one person stumble over the sum and another get impatient, then go back and help. By afternoon the saying had softened at its edges, the way told things do. A child kept the note going while an older neighbor finished the sentence. There was no bell to mark the moment the news became theirs. The note was still in the beams when word came up the pass: the bitter pie had heard it. He had understood it. He had stopped waiting. Boof felt the tremor before she heard the messenger's feet. Above her, the pegs held; dust drifted from a beam. She checked the sling.

entries.label: Boof
entries.text: "Is this where the trail terminates?" Boof asked the king-post. The Fool answered with a soft knock on the honest oak — no. A true test does not end a story; it only takes away the story's excuses. Everyone in the valley now knew what the wish cost small and what it cost grand, and one bitter pie had decided the arithmetic applied to other people. Nothing grew in Bone.land that had not been carried in. In her sling, beside the egg, the slice from Bonk City was still warm through its paper. She had carried it over the pass without eating it. She did not know why, and she did not take it out. She settled the egg deeper against her chest and turned south. Behind her, the timber answered the shaking with small creaks, peg to socket, joint to joist. Ahead, the road looked much as it had that morning. She went carefully.

entries.label: Boof
entries.text: It happened between one honest sniff and the next. On the road out of Bone.land, where the frame's note still hung in the air, Mr. BaneWAP stopped shadowing and simply took — banker's crust cracking with the effort, tin lockbox open and shut, the egg gone from Boof's sling before her growl could finish forming. He did not run far. He did not need to. He stood on a low rise with the warm shell in both crimped hands and wished the wish he had been drafting since the auction failed: an empire, whole, at once. And the wish — this is the part no one had priced — granted instantly. It was a moment of bloom before seed . Karmic momentum does not refuse a grand wish. It simply pays it out the way momentum pays everything: one coincidence at a time, minimum-viable, corrections deferred. A barn deed blew against his crust. A road bent to end at his feet. A distant clerk misfiled a fortune in his name. The empire arrived. It arrived mediocre. His empire arrived in pieces: throne first, banners after, subjects caught halfway through errands. One still held a loaf. The throne smelled rented. The banners hung in colors nobody had ordered. Boof watched the new emperor wait for the scene to feel complete. It kept arriving. It never did.

entries.label: Bloom
entries.text: Deep beneath his crust, a berry woke. The wish had passed through him, leaving its drop of light just as it had in the fields. One seam shone, then another. Warmth worked through the bitter filling. He tasted what he had kept from everyone, himself included. Sweet. It had been sweet all along. Around him, the banners stirred. He made a small sound the throne did nothing to support.

entries.label: The Fool
entries.text: The Midas touch, sampled: everything he grasped turned to more, and none of it to enough. Sound it, send it back sweeter. That is the whole law. He tapped the rented throne once — hollow — and let the note say what the timber had: interest is owed on every borrowed want.

entries.label: The Wish That Would Not Finish
entries.text: Here is the paradox the timber had circled without naming: a wish only leaves its shell when it is finished, and a wish the size of an empire is never finishable. There is always one more coincidence owed, one more correction pending in some far county where a stranger's luck must be bent to balance a king's. The grant kept arriving and kept not being done. The empire stood, hollow as a rented crown, and the egg in BaneWAP's hands stayed exactly as warm as it had been in the frozen furrow — spent and unspent at once, a note held but not released. At the edge of the new court, a woman still holding her market basket asked whether she could go home. A banner brushed her shoulder. No one answered; the emperor was staring at his own hands. Boof could smell bread cooling in the basket and dust rising where the throne had scraped the ground. The empire needed this woman to be a subject. She needed to get the bread indoors before rain. Boof watched her take one step backward, then another. The banner lifted, and she slipped beneath it. His crimped hands softened. The egg slipped, tipped, rolled down the rise, past a banner dragging in the dust. Boof stepped forward. It came to rest against her paws, warm as ever. The crack had widened enough to show gold within. She checked the shell with her nose. Still humming. Still waiting. That night, wherever she set the sling down, the ground beneath it was busy by morning: torch-lines bent toward the shell from every root within reach, and the frost drew back a hand's width, as if something under the loam had been given more to work with. Whatever was in the egg, it was not keeping its warmth to itself.

entries.label: The Fool
entries.text: Eight honks sounded. The ninth still sleeps in the shell. Small wishes travel farthest. He pointed downhill to two rivers that had not yet agreed to forget their springs, and Boof — who finally almost knew her want — went to meet them.

entries.label: Boof
entries.text: Two great mountain rivers met beneath a wide, low-planked timber bridge, and it was there, muzzle over the rail with the egg warm between her paws, that Boof finally knew. Not a hunch. Not the shape of a want seen sideways. She knew, the way a true scent is known at its end, and the wish was small enough to hold in a mouth: that the land keep one warm furrow open — always — for whatever arrives next without a receipt. Below her the waters ran in an unblended seam — berry-dark and chalk-pale sharing one bed without forgetting their springs — and she understood that her wish was the same shape as the river: a membrane, not a merger. Room made, nothing owned. The Off-Season Genie had followed her since the third chamber, because her wants were too small for instruments built for emperors. He heard it and went very still — the way a craftsman goes still when the one job his tools were never sized for turns out to be the job he stayed retired for. The Genie counted the price onto the rail. Once, he'd said a small wish cost a coincidence and a Thursday. This one asked for always. He emptied what remained in his reserve and kept his hand open beside it. “Everything left,” he said. “Plus one Thursday.” Boof looked from his hand to his face. Neither bargained.

entries.label: Path
entries.text: Far upcountry, frost loosened along one furrow. The ground warmed and stayed warm. That night the ants moved beneath it. With less heat to make, they could tend more roots; their torch-lines ran farther along the furrow than they had in years, and a beetle who had been cold since autumn found a lit street. The berry rows widened through the winter. The ants had known the Genie longer than anyone, and they were the only ones who noticed what always had cost him. A stranger would receive a good coincidence. Somewhere in the coming week, a Thursday quietly went missing. On the bridge, no thunder. Only water under wood, and the Genie putting his empty hand away.

entries.label: The Fool
entries.text: The last-wish trope, sampled: the genie spends the final granting on himself — and he does not fade. He posts himself to the grove and accrues. Spent to the last coin of himself, the Off-Season Genie walked upstream into the grove that keeps echoes, and became its next one — a granting you can visit.

entries.label: Both Receipts Posted
entries.text: Then the last threads came down the road to the bridge, because a confluence gathers. Mr. BaneWAP arrived first, walking soft, his banker's crust gone flaky and generous where the awakened berries had re-sweetened him from the inside out. He had no coin fit for the apology he owed, so he paid in the only currency a pie has: he split himself, clean down the crimp, and offered the slices to the road. And Mr. BoonWAP — who serves himself in slices and is never smaller — received him warm, the way Bonk City receives everything, and showed him the trick of it: giving is not subtraction if the filling is true. Mx. BoneWAP arrived last, clean-boiled and exact, and pinned both receipts to the bridge rail where any traveler could read them: one slice given in apology, one slice received in welcome, sources named, nothing flattened. And here was the quiet miracle of the small wish already at work — both receipts could hang side by side, because the wish had aligned them. The whole confluence held: berry water and chalk water, bitter pie and boon pie, hall and grove, all sharing one bed along a living seam, a membrane that shares without giving the house away. The egg in Boof's sling was lighter now, and its heartbeat had changed from waiting to arriving. Boof listened to the travelers crossing behind her, the different weights of their steps, the pause where someone stopped to look down. Under the bridge, one river carried a darker thread for a while before the currents loosened it. She followed the color as far as she could. Upstream lay the places each had come from, still there even after she could no longer tell the waters apart. The egg rested easily in its sling. For the first time in days, she shifted her shoulder without arranging it around a weight.

entries.label: Boof
entries.text: "Where does a spent wish go?" Boof asked the twilight, nose lifted toward the archive downstream. Nowhere, said the warm wind off the far furrow. It stays. It becomes a place you can stand. Boof followed the gravel path downstream. The egg rode lightly now, its song rising through sack and strap. Eight notes behind her, one gathering under her chin. Beyond the bend stood the archive. She could hear the river through its open door.

entries.label: Boof
entries.text: The round room at the end of the river path was smaller and quieter than any map had promised, and it was here, on the polished slate at the center of the rotunda, that the finished wish did the one last thing a finished wish is required to do. It sounded. The ninth honk — the one the Fool had carried unsounded through eight chambers of sampled tropes, the shard that had slept in the shell since before the frost — left the egg as one clean note and rolled out over the whole land at once. Over the dawnward field and its one kept furrow, over the grove with its newest echo, over Bonk City serving itself in slices, over Bone.land's honest joists, over two rivers sharing a bed without forgetting their springs. Boof stood in the middle of it with her ears full of gold and understood that she was hearing a return path made of sound: every trope the set had sampled, coming home changed, with interest. And when the note settled, the maps — the same maps that had beaded and refused since the first morning — finally took the ink. The first line they accepted, before any border or crown, was the warm furrow. Nobody wrote it. The land set it down itself, line by line, having at last agreed to know what had happened to it. Beside the great book stood a bowl of cold spring water. Boof drank. The dust of the journey washed from her throat. On the nearest shelf lay two copies of a map. In one, a white thread of path ran between a garden wall and the river. In the smaller copy, the lines touched. Someone had penciled in the margin: leave room for the path. Boof sniffed the first page. Wet grass. She sniffed the second. Only paper.

entries.label: Record
entries.text: The great book lay open. No one stood over it. An oath. An apology. A genie's whole reserve, and one Thursday besides. The pages held what each had cost. Boof had carried a want until she knew its shape. Now the wish was spent and the note had sounded. On the desk sat the shell. Empty. Light. She nosed its rim. Still warm.

entries.label: The Fool
entries.text: Thirteen chambers, nine honks, and every borrowed trope gone home changed — warmer than it left. The Boonberry Fool bowed, and for once said nothing clever. He set each borrowed thing back where it belonged: the found egg, warmer; the greedy wish, sweeter; the echo, somewhere you can visit; the small wish, a furrow that never closes; and the happily-ever-after, changed — an ever-after that leaves its last line blank.

entries.label: The Blank Last Line
entries.text: Boof looked from the book to the open shell-shaped door. The first map had refused her egg. This one held the road she had walked, all the way back to the warm furrow. She followed it with her nose. Grove, gate, river bend. Here was a place she had been afraid. Here, a place she had eaten. At the end, one line stayed blank. Every other page in the book had been glassed — pressed clear and kept, season over season, the older lines still legible under the new. This one page had never been. That was why it could still take a line. The Fool waited. The pen waited. Nothing came. At last he set the empty shell beside the line, ready for the next wish. The shelves had room. The door stayed open.

entries.label: Boof
entries.text: Boof rested her chin beside the shell. Its warmth reached through the wood. Outside, a cart rattled past. A bell rang once. She lifted an ear. Nearby, this time. It stayed nearby. Morning spread across the farms. Smoke rose from kitchens; someone would soon be cutting bread. Far off, one furrow steamed in the frost. Boof turned toward the door. She lingered with her nose just beyond the arch, where the cool air met the room's last warmth. The road smelled of damp gravel, horse, a little spilled grain. Behind those came the less certain scents of places she had not visited. Nobody called her back to explain the ending. Inside, the Fool moved a chair away from the desk so there would be room to approach it. Boof heard the legs scrape, then settle. She waited until the cart had passed before stepping into the road. Where its dust settled, a hat hung in the air at the height of a person's head — round-crowned, brimmed, touching nothing. It was a little farther down the road each time she looked. She could not smell who was under it. She could smell that someone was. Behind her, the shell kept warm. The last line waited.
